title: Vulnerability that lets hackers SSH into Linux devices is under active exploitation
gist: A critical OpenSSH and musl vulnerability, CVE-2026-123158 (*sshole), is under active exploitation within days of disclosure, including by a group tracked as GT10 using an apparently AI-generated backdoor. Alpine Linux systems are especially exposed, and OpenSSH has released a fix.

insights.claim: The *sshole vulnerability (CVE-2026-123158) became public last Thursday and was being actively exploited four days later, with Greynoise, watchTowr and Previdian all reporting attacks.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Exploitation within days shows patch windows are collapsing; unpatched Linux fleets are at immediate risk.

insights.claim: Greynoise says a group it tracks as GT10 conducted 'mature intrusions' against its Southeast Asia honeypots, using a backdoor called TAC Agent that has Chinese-language comments and appears to be AI-generated.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: AI-assisted malware development is lowering the bar for capable attackers.

insights.claim: TAC Agent supports shell commands, system reconnaissance and persistence, and GT10 installs Python3 on machines lacking it because the backdoor requires it.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Unexpected Python installs are a usable detection signal.

insights.claim: watchTowr observed exploitation tied to botnets and cryptocurrency, and Previdian recorded 20 exploitation attempts from 13 unique IPs across nine countries.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Opportunistic, multi-actor exploitation signals broad scanning, including crypto-mining motives.

insights.claim: The flaw arises when OpenSSH runs with musl, without PAM, on systems with a SHA256/SHA512-hashed password account and a passwordless account marked '*' in /etc/shadow, a standard setup for some account types.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Conditions are specific but common, so exposure is concentrated in particular distributions.

insights.claim: Passwords longer than 256 characters sent to a passwordless account cause musl's hashing function to return '*', which OpenSSH misinterprets as a valid password hash, per Red Hat.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: A simple input-length edge case yields unauthenticated privileged access.

insights.claim: Despite its multiple preconditions, the bug threatens a large base of machines, most notably Alpine Linux, and attackers can identify vulnerable servers among millions exposed to the Internet in seconds.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Container-heavy Alpine deployments make the supply-chain blast radius large.

insights.claim: OpenSSH has released a fix, and users should install it promptly while musl users should investigate further.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Patching urgency; endpoint and cloud security vendors may see demand.
